Just now

--

Code generation is now free. Code comprehension is not. Here is how to survive the Pull Request bottleneck.
Three months ago, a mid-level engineer on my team opened a Pull Request on a Tuesday afternoon.
I looked at the diff and my stomach dropped. 45 files changed. 3,200 lines of code added. 0 lines deleted.
I checked the Jira ticket. He had picked it up right after standup. It had taken him less than four hours to “write” a PR that would take a Senior Engineer at least two solid days to review responsibly. When I asked him about the implementation details of a specific state-management file, he hesitated, then said, “Cursor handled the boilerplate for that part. It works locally.”
Welcome to software engineering in 2026.
We have successfully solved the problem of typing. AI agents can spit out thousands of lines of syntactically correct code in minutes. But we have slammed face-first into a new, much more dangerous bottleneck: The Asymmetry of AI.
Code generation has become exponentially cheaper and faster. But human reading speed, cognitive load, and architectural comprehension haven’t changed since the 1990s.
As an Engineering Manager, if you apply traditional code review processes to AI-generated code, your senior engineers will burn out in a month. They will become full-time readers of AI slop.
We have to completely rewrite the rules of the Pull Request. Here is the framework I use to manage AI-assisted development teams without sacrificing production stability.
The 3 Deadly Sins of AI PRs
Before you can fix the review process, you have to understand exactly how AI fails. AI doesn’t write “bad” code in the traditional sense. It writes code with “plausible deniability.” It looks clean, the variables are named well, but it hides structural rot.
When reviewing an AI-heavy PR, you are looking for three specific sins:

• Architectural Drift: AI has a localized brain. If you ask it to build a feature, it will often build the infrastructure for that feature inside the component, ignoring the global utility functions your team spent three months building. It creates silos of duplicated logic.

• The “Happy Path” Bias: AI models are optimists. They write beautiful code for when the API returns a 200 OK. They are notoriously terrible at writing defensive code, handling edge-case state, or managing retry logic for network failures.

• The Context Collapse: If an AI forgets the exact shape of your database schema during generation, it will quietly invent one that fits its immediate needs, resulting in massive type mismatches at runtime.
The New Rules of AI Code Reviews
To survive the volume of AI-generated code, you must stop acting like a line-editor and start acting like a Systems Auditor.
Rule 1: No Tests, No Review (The Hard Gate)
In the pre-AI era, we often reviewed the code first, and then reminded the developer, “Hey, add some unit tests for this before we merge.”
You can no longer do this. If an AI wrote the code, the developer must use the AI to write the tests. Because AI is deterministic in its context window, if it hallucinates a business rule in the code, it will write a test that passes that hallucination.
The fix: Mandate Test-Driven Development (TDD). The human engineer must write the test cases (or strictly define the parameters) before the AI generates the logic. When I review a PR, I read the *.test.ts files first. If the tests are comprehensive, I trust the AI's implementation 80% more. If there are no tests, the PR is instantly rejected.
Rule 2: Review the Prompt, Not Just the Code
If a developer cannot explain how they asked the AI to build something, they don’t understand what was built.
We updated our PR templates to require a “Prompt Context” section. I don’t want to see the raw transcript, but I want to know the constraints the engineer applied.
Did they say: “Build a shopping cart”? (Danger). Or did they say: “Implement a cart component. Use the existing useCartStore Zustand hook. Do not add any new API routes; use the trpc mutations already defined in /server/routers." (Safe).
Rule 3: Automate the Syntax, Humanize the Architecture
Senior engineers should not be checking for missing semicolons, unused variables, or bad formatting. If you don’t have aggressive linters, Prettier, and static analysis tools running in your CI/CD pipeline, AI will bury you in nitpicks.
Configure your CI pipeline to auto-reject PRs that lower test coverage, introduce any types in TypeScript, or fail cyclomatic complexity checks. Reserve the human brain for answering one question: "Does this fit our system design?"
Rule 4: Small PRs or Pair Reviews
AI makes it incredibly easy to pile 30 features into one PR. Enforce strict limits on diff sizes. If a developer uses an agent to refactor 50 files, do not attempt to review it asynchronously. Jump on a 15-minute call, have the developer share their screen, and make them walk you through the data flow. If they can’t, it doesn’t ship.
The AI-Ready PR Template
Here is the exact Pull Request template my team uses. Feel free to copy this into your .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md:
## 🚀 What does this PR do?
[Explain the business logic and goal]## 🤖 AI Assistance & Prompt Context
- [ ] No AI was used for this PR.
- [ ] AI (Cursor/Copilot) was used.
**If used, summarize the core constraints given to the AI:**
> *Example: "Instructed Claude to build the data table using our internal UI library and strictly map to the Zod schema in `types.ts`."*
## 🏗️ Architectural Checklist
- [ ] Does this duplicate any existing global utilities?
- [ ] Are all new dependencies absolutely necessary?
- [ ] Have edge cases (loading, error states, network failure) been accounted for?
## 🧪 Testing
- [ ] Human-verified unit tests are included and passing.
- [ ] I can personally explain every line of logic the AI generated.
The Evolution of the Senior Engineer
There is a growing sentiment that AI coding agents will replace software engineers. I strongly disagree. But it will replace engineers who only know how to type syntax.
The software engineer of the future is an editor. An architect. A reviewer.
Your job as a Tech Lead or Engineering Manager is to build the guardrails the automated tests, the CI/CD checks, the strict architectural patterns so that your team can run at 100mph with AI without driving the company off a cliff.
Stop trying to read every line of AI code. Start verifying the systems that generated it.
What is your strategy? How has your team adapted to the flood of AI-generated code in PRs? Drop a comment below, I’d love to hear how other EMs are handling the noise.
